title: Poison-then-Hide: Finetuning-Activated Backdoor Attack on Pretrained Vision Encoders
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A dormant backdoor planted in a pretrained model stays hidden through clean behavior and is activated only by later benign finetuning.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right, encoder/head stacks with lock and status icons
description: A pale-yellow panel titled 'Finetuning-Activated Attack' shows three stages left to right. Stage 1 is the source dataset (ImageNet photos of a kitten and fruit) feeding a gray Pretrained Encoder and Source Head, ending in 'Clean Pretraining' with a green checkmark. Stage 2 is a red 'Attack' column with a devil icon and the steps 'Optimize Trigger, Poison Encoder, Hide Backdoor'. It feeds a pink encoder with a closed lock and a devil icon, over a gray Target Head, and its output is 'Clean Output Given Unactivated Backdoor'. Stage 3 is the target dataset (RESISC satellite images) feeding a deeper pink encoder with an open lock and a red Target Head. It ends in 'Clean Finetuning Activates Hidden Backdoor', and an arrow points to 'Backdoor Output During Inference' with a devil icon. Red text and shading mark the attack, and gray marks benign components. Black arrows connect the stages.
caption: Setting of finetuning-activated attacks. Checkmark icons denote clean behavior, evil-head icons denote backdoor behavior, and lock icons denote activation.
abstract: Backdoor attacks threaten the integrity of machine learning models by allowing attackers to control model behavior through triggers. Models can be compromised during finetuning by backdoor attacks through either poisoned data or adversarial training objectives. Because existing finetuning-activated attacks assume limited domain shift or frozen encoder layers, they often fail under full-model finetuning. We target a stealthy finetuning-activated attack where a dormant backdoor is implanted in a pretrained encoder, and later activated by finetuning on clean downstream data. We propose Poison-then-Hide, a novel attack that remains effective when the entire model is finetuned in a domain transfer. Our approach consists of three components: trigger optimization, base encoder poisoning, and targeted unlearning to conceal the backdoor. We evaluate our method on six datasets and three model architectures, and achieve state-of-the-art (up to 97%) attack success rates. We find that jointly learning the benign target task alongside the poisoning is critical to the attack's success. We demonstrate standard detection and mitigation defenses cannot fully remove the backdoor, which can reappear after benign finetuning.
